L6@P0: Abstract. We introduce a new approach to realize incrementally verifiable computation (IVC), in which the prover recursively proves the correct
L7@P0: execution of incremental computations of the form y = F()
L8@P0: (x), where F is
L9@P0: a (potentially non-deterministic) computation, x is the input, y is the output, and > 0. Unlike prior approaches to realize IVC, our approach avoids
L10@P0: succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (SNARKs) entirely and
L11@P0: arguments of knowledge in general. Instead, we introduce and employ folding schemes, a weaker, simpler, and more efficiently-realizable primitive,
L12@P0: which reduces the task of checking two instances in some relation to the
L13@P0: task of checking a single instance. We construct a folding scheme for a characterization of NP and show that it implies an IVC scheme with improved
L14@P0: efficiency characteristics: (1) the “recursion overhead” (i.e., the number of
L15@P0: steps that the prover proves in addition to proving the execution of F) is a
L16@P0: constant and it is dominated by two group scalar multiplications expressed
L17@P0: as a circuit (this is the smallest recursion overhead in the literature), and
L18@P0: (2) the prover’s work at each step is dominated by two multiexponentiations of size O(|F|), providing the fastest prover in the literature. The size
L19@P0: of a proof is O(|F|) group elements, but we show that using a variant of
L20@P0: an existing zkSNARK, the prover can prove the knowledge of a valid proof
L21@P0: succinctly and in zero-knowledge with O(log |F|) group elements. Finally,
L22@P0: our approach neither requires a trusted setup nor FFTs, so it can be instantiated efficiently with any cycles of elliptic curves where DLOG is hard.
L23@P0: 1 Introduction
L24@P0: We revisit the problem of realizing incrementally-verifiable computation (IVC)
L25@P0: [43]: a cryptographic primitive that enables producing proofs of correct execution
L26@P0: of “long running” computations such that a verifier can efficiently verify the correct
L27@P0: execution of any prefix of the computation. IVC enables a wide variety of applications including verifiable delay functions [9,45], succinct blockchains [13,31], and
L28@P0: incrementally-verifiable versions of verifiable state machines [33,39].
L29@P0: A well-known approach to construct IVC is to use succinct non-interactive
L30@P0: arguments of knowledge (SNARKs) for NP [23,24,29,36]: at each incremental step
L31@P0: i, the prover produces a SNARK proving that it has applied F correctly to the output of step i−1 and that the SNARK verifier represented as a circuit has accepted
L32@P0: c International Association for Cryptologic Research 2022
L33@P0: Y. Dodis and T. Shrimpton (Eds.): CRYPTO 2022, LNCS 13510, pp. 359–388, 2022.
L34@P0-1: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-15985-5_13360 A. Kothapalli et al.
L35@P1: the SNARK from step i − 1[6,8]. However, it is well-known that this approach is
L36@P1: impractical [6,19]. Alternatively, one can use SNARKs without trusted setup [17,
L37@P1: 21,38,41] but their verifiers are more expensive than those of SNARKs with trusted
L38@P1: setup, both asymptotically and concretely. Recent works [10,12,15,16] aim to
L39@P1: address the inefficiency of SNARK-based IVC, with an innovative approach: at
L40@P1: each step, the verifier circuit “defers” expensive steps in verifying a SNARK for
L41@P1: NP instances (e.g., verifying polynomial evaluation proofs) by accumulating those
L42@P1: steps into a single instance that is later checked efficiently. However, these works
L43@P1: still require the prover to produce a SNARK at each step and the verifier circuit
L44@P1: to partially verify that SNARK.
L45@P1: We introduce a new approach that avoids SNARKs (and more generally arguments of knowledge) entirely and relies purely on deferral to realize IVC. In a
L46@P1: nutshell, instead of accumulating expensive steps of verifying a SNARK for NP
L47@P1: instances, the verifier circuit in our approach accumulates the NP instances themselves. We formalize this technique as a new and minimal primitive, which we refer
L48@P1: to as a folding scheme. A folding scheme is weaker, simpler, and far more efficient
L49@P1: compared to arguments of knowledge including SNARKs. Indeed, realizing IVC
L50@P1: via folding schemes results in improved efficiency over prior work (Fig. 3): (1) the
L51@P1: verifier circuit is constant-sized and its size is dominated by two group scalar multiplications; this is the smallest verifier circuit in the literature (in the context of
L52@P1: recursive proof composition); and (2) the prover’s work at each step is dominated
L53@P1: by two multiexponentiations of size O(|F|), providing the fastest prover in the literature, both asymptotically and concretely. Section 1.4 provides a detailed comparison between our approach and prior work.
L54@P1: 1.1 Folding Schemes
L55@P1: A folding scheme is defined with respect to an NP relation, and it is a protocol between an untrusted prover and a verifier. Both entities hold two N-sized
L56@P1: NP instances, and the prover in addition holds purported witnesses for both
L57@P1: instances. The protocol enables the prover and the verifier to output a single
L58@P1: N-sized NP instance, which we refer to as a folded instance. Furthermore, the
L59@P1: prover privately outputs a purported witness to the folded instance using purported witnesses for the original instances. Informally, a folding scheme guarantees
L60@P1: that the folded instance is satisfiable only if the original instances are satisfiable.
L61@P1: A folding scheme is said to be non-trivial if the verifier’s costs and the communication are lower in the case where the verifier participates in the folding scheme and
L62@P1: then verifies a purported NP witness for the folded instance than the case where
L63@P1: the verifier verifies purported NP witnesses for each of the original instances.
L64@P1: Several existing techniques exhibit the two-to-one reduction pattern of folding
L65@P1: schemes. Examples include the sumcheck protocol [35] and the split-and-fold
L66@P1: techniques in inner product arguments [11]. [30, App. A] provides further details.
L67@P1: Remark 1 (Folding Schemes vs. SNARKs). SNARKs for NP [7,23,24,29,36]
L68@P1: trivially imply a folding scheme for NP: given two NP instances u1 and u2 and
L69@P1: the corresponding witnesses, the prover proves u1 by producing a SNARK. The
L70@P1-2: verifier checks that SNARK and then sets u2 to be the folded instance. However,Nova: Recursive Zero-Knowledge Arguments from Folding Schemes 361
L71@P2: we construct a folding scheme for NP without relying on SNARKs (or more generally arguments of knowledge). Specifically, our folding scheme is weaker than
L72@P2: any argument of knowledge (succinct or otherwise) because it merely reduces the
L73@P2: satisfiability of two NP instances to the satisfiability of a single NP instance.1
L74@P2: To design a folding scheme for NP, we start with a popular NP-complete language that generalizes arithmetic circuit satisfiability: R1CS (Definition 10). As
L75@P2: we illustrate later, it is difficult to devise a folding scheme for R1CS. To address
L76@P2: this, we introduce a variant of R1CS, called relaxed R1CS, which, like R1CS,
L77@P2: not only characterizes NP, but, unlike R1CS, can support a folding scheme. The
L78@P2: following theorem captures the cryptographic and efficiency characteristics of
L79@P2: our folding scheme for relaxed R1CS.
L80@P2: Theorem 1. There exists a constant-round, public-coin, zero-knowledge folding
L81@P2: scheme for relaxed R1CS where for N-sized relaxed R1CS instances over a finite
L82@P2: field F with the same “structure” (i.e., R1CS coefficient matrices), the prover’s
L83@P2: work is Oλ(N), and the verifier’s work and the communication are both Oλ(1),
L84@P2: assuming the existence of any additively-homomorphic commitment scheme that
L85@P2: provides Oλ(1)-sized commitments to N-sized vectors over F (e.g., Pedersen’s
L86@P2: commitments), where λ is the security parameter.
L87@P2: Because our folding scheme is public coin, it can be made non-interactive in
L88@P2: the random oracle model using the Fiat-Shamir transform [22], and be instantiated (heuristically) in the standard model using a concrete hash function. We
L89@P2: rely on such a non-interactive folding scheme to construct IVC.
L90@P2: 1.2 IVC from Non-interactive Folding Schemes
L91@P2: We show how to realize IVC using a non-interactive version of our folding scheme
L92@P2: for relaxed R1CS. We refer to our construction as Nova.
L93@P2: Recall that an IVC is an argument of knowledge [29,36]
L94@P2: 2 for incremental
L95@P2: computations of the form y = F()
L96@P2: (x), where F is a (possibly non-deterministic)
L97@P2: computation, > 0, x is a public input, and y is the public output. At each
L98@P2: incremental step, the IVC prover produces a proof that the step was computed
L99@P2: correctly and it has verified a proof for the prior step. In other words, at each
L100@P2: incremental step, the IVC prover produces a proof of satisfiability for an augmented circuit that augments the circuit for F with a “verifier circuit” that
L101@P2: verifies the proof of the prior step. Recursively, the final proof proves the correctness of the entire incremental computation. A key aspect of IVC is that
L102@P2: neither the IVC verifier’s work nor the IVC proof size depends on the number of
L103@P2: 1 This work realizes IVC using our folding scheme. As IVC implies SNARKs (e.g.,
L104@P2: see [6]), one might wonder whether folding schemes are in general weaker than
L105@P2: SNARKs. However, existing constructions of IVC (including our own) rely on additional assumptions (§4.2), which the resulting IVC-based SNARK inherits. 2 An argument of knowledge for circuit satisfiability enables an untrusted polynomialtime prover to prove to a verifier the knowledge of a witness w such that C(w, x)= y,
L106@P2-3: where C is a circuit, x is some public input, and y is some public output.362 A. Kothapalli et al.
L107@P3: steps in the incremental computation. In particular, the IVC verifier only verifies
L108@P3: the proof produced at the last step of the incremental computation.
L109@P3: In Nova, we consider incremental computations, where each step of the incremental computation is expressed with R1CS (all the steps in the incremental
L110@P3: computation share the same R1CS coefficient matrices). At step i of the incremental computation, as in other approaches to IVC, Nova’s prover proves that
L111@P3: the step i was computed correctly. Furthermore, at step i, instead of verifying a
L112@P3: proof for step i−1 (as in traditional approaches to IVC), Nova’s approach treats
L113@P3: the computation at step i−1 as an R1CS instance and folds that into a running
L114@P3: relaxed R1CS instance. Specifically, at each step, Nova’s prover proves that it has
L115@P3: performed the step’s computation and has folded its prior step represented as an
L116@P3: R1CS instance into a running relaxed R1CS instance. In other words, the circuit
L117@P3: satisfiability instance that the prover proves at each incremental step computes
L118@P3: a step of the incremental computation and includes a circuit for the computation
L119@P3: of the verifier in the non-interactive folding scheme for relaxed R1CS.
L120@P3: A distinctive aspect of Nova’s approach to IVC is that it achieves the smallest
L121@P3: “verifier circuit” in the literature. Since the verifier’s costs in the non-interactive
L122@P3: version of the folding scheme for relaxed R1CS is Oλ(1), the size of the computation that Nova’s prover proves at each incremental step is ≈|F|, assuming Nsized vectors are committed with an Oλ(1)-sized commitments (e.g., Pedersen’s
L123@P3: commitments). In particular, the verifier circuit in Nova is constant-sized and
L124@P3: its size is dominated by two group scalar multiplications. Furthermore, Nova’s
L125@P3: prover’s work at each step is dominated by two multiexponentiations of size ≈|F|.
L126@P3: Note that Nova’s prover does not perform any FFTs, so it can be instantiated
L127@P3: efficiently using any cycles of elliptic curves where DLOG is hard.
L128@P3: With the description thus far, the size of an IVC proof (which is a purported
L129@P3: witness for the running relaxed R1CS instance) is Oλ(|F|). Instead of sending
L130@P3: such a proof to a verifier, at any point in the incremental computation, Nova’s
L131@P3: prover can prove the knowledge of a satisfying witness to the running relaxed
L132@P3: R1CS instance in zero-knowledge with an Oλ(log |F|)-sized succinct proof using

L198: # Nova: High-speed recursive arguments from folding schemes
L199: 
L200: Nova is a high-speed recursive SNARK (a SNARK is type cryptographic proof system that enables a prover to prove a mathematical statement to a verifier with a short proof and succinct verification, and a recursive SNARK enables producing proofs that prove statements about prior proofs).
L201: More precisely, Nova achieves 【82†incrementally verifiable computation (IVC)†iacr.org】, a powerful cryptographic primitive that allows a prover to produce a proof of correct execution of a "long running" sequential computations in an incremental fashion. For example, IVC enables the following: The prover takes as input a proof $\pi_i$ proving the first $i$ steps of its computation and then update it to produce a proof $\pi_{i+1}$ proving the correct execution of the first $i + 1$ steps.
L202: Crucially, the prover's work to update the proof does not depend on the number of steps executed thus far, and the verifier's work to verify a proof does not grow with the number of steps in the computation. IVC schemes including Nova have a wide variety of applications such as Rollups, verifiable delay functions (VDFs), succinct blockchains, incrementally verifiable versions of 【83†verifiable state machines†eprint.iacr.org】, and, more generally, proofs of (virtual) machine executions (e.g., EVM, RISC-V).
L203: A distinctive aspect of Nova is that it is the simplest recursive proof system in the literature, yet it provides the fastest prover. Furthermore, it achieves the smallest verifier circuit (a key metric to minimize in this context): the circuit is constant-sized and its size is about 10,000 multiplication gates. Nova is constructed from a simple primitive called a folding scheme, a cryptographic primitive that reduces the task of checking two NP statements into the task of checking a single NP statement.
L204: ## Details of the library
L205: 
L206: This repository provides `nova-snark,` a Rust library implementation of Nova over a cycle of elliptic curves. Our code supports three curve cycles: (1) Pallas/Vesta, (2) BN254/Grumpkin, and (3) secp/secq.
L207: At its core, Nova relies on a commitment scheme for vectors. Compressing IVC proofs using Spartan relies on interpreting commitments to vectors as commitments to multilinear polynomials and prove evaluations of committed polynomials. Our code implements three commitment schemes and evaluation arguments:
L208:   1. Pedersen commitments with IPA-based evaluation argument (supported on all three curve cycles)
L209:   2. HyperKZG commitments and evaluation argument (supported on curves with pairings, e.g., BN254)
L210:   3. Mercury commitments and evaluation argument (supported on curves with pairings, e.g., BN254) - Mercury is an optimized variant that provides faster verification than HyperKZG
L211: For more details on using HyperKZG or Mercury, please see the test `test_ivc_nontrivial_with_compression`. Both HyperKZG and Mercury require a universal setup (the so-called "powers of tau"). See the 【84†Universal Setup】 section below for details on loading setup parameters.
L212: We also implement a SNARK, based on 【85†Spartan†eprint.iacr.org】, to compress IVC proofs produced by Nova. There are two variants, one that does not use any preprocessing and another that uses preprocessing of circuits to ensure that the verifier's run time does not depend on the size of the step circuit. The preprocessing variant of Spartan is called MicroSpartan and is described in the 【86†MicroNova†eprint.iacr.org】 paper.
L213: Prior to compression, the IVC proof is folded with a random instance, which makes the proof zero-knowledge. The details of this technique are described in the HyperNova paper.
L214: ## Supported front-ends
L215: 
L216: A front-end is a tool to take a high-level program and turn it into an intermediate representation (e.g., a circuit) that can be used to prove executions of the program on concrete inputs. There are three supported ways to write high-level programs in a form that can be proven with Nova.
L217: 
L218:   1. The native APIs of Nova accept circuits expressed with bellman-style circuits. See 【87†minroot.rs】 or 【88†sha256.rs】 for examples.
L219:   2. Circom: A DSL and a compiler to transform high-level program expressed in its language into a circuit. There exist middleware to turn output of circom into a form suitable for proving with Nova. See 【89†Nova Scotia】 and 【90†Circom Scotia】. In the future, we will add examples in the Nova repository to use these tools with Nova.
L220: ## Cargo Features
L221: 
L222: The library provides several optional features:
L223: 
L224: Feature  | Description
L225: --- | ---
L226: `io` (default)  | Enables loading commitment keys from Powers of Tau files
L227: `evm`  | Enables EVM-friendly serialization
L228: `experimental`  | Enables experimental features like NeutronNova
L229: `test-utils`  | Enables insecure test utilities (random tau generation) - do not use in production
L230: Example usage:
L231: 
L232:     # Default features (includes io)
L233:     cargo build
L234: 
L235:     # With EVM verifier support
L236:     cargo build --features evm
L237: 
L238:     # With experimental NeutronNova
L239:     cargo build --features experimental
L240: ## Tests and examples
L241: 
L242: By default, we enable the `asm` feature of an underlying library (which boosts performance by up to 50%). If the library fails to build or run, one can pass `--no-default-features` to `cargo` commands noted below.

L247:     `

L249: To run an example:

L252:     `
L253: ## References
L254: 
L255: The following paper, which appeared at CRYPTO 2022, provides details of the Nova proof system and a proof of security:
L256: 
L257: 【91†Nova: Recursive Zero-Knowledge Arguments from Folding Schemes†eprint.iacr.org】
L258: Abhiram Kothapalli, Srinath Setty, and Ioanna Tzialla
L259: CRYPTO 2022
L260: 
L261: For efficiency, our implementation of the Nova proof system is instantiated over a cycle of elliptic curves. The following paper specifies that instantiation and provides a proof of security:
L262: 【92†Revisiting the Nova Proof System on a Cycle of Curves†eprint.iacr.org】
L263: Wilson Nguyen, Dan Boneh, and Srinath Setty
L264: IACR ePrint 2023/969
L265: 
L266: The zero-knowledge property is achieved using an idea described in the following paper:
L267: 
L268: 【93†HyperNova: Recursive arguments for customizable constraint systems†eprint.iacr.org】
L269: Abhiram Kothapalli and Srinath Setty
L270: CRYPTO 2024
L271: The following paper describes an on-chain efficient version of Nova. We have open-sourced components of MicroNova including the HyperKZG polynomial commitment scheme and the MicroSpartan SNARK (which is provided in 【94†ppsnark.rs】):
L272: 
L273: 【86†MicroNova: Folding-based arguments with efficient (on-chain) verification†eprint.iacr.org】
L274: Jiaxing Zhao, Srinath Setty, Weidong Cui, and Greg Zaverucha
L275: IEEE S&P 2025
L276: ### Experimental: NeutronNova
L277: 
L278: The library includes an experimental implementation of NeutronNova. Enable with `--features experimental`. Note that experimental features may have breaking changes between releases.
L279: ## Universal Setup for HyperKZG and Mercury
L280: 
L281: HyperKZG and Mercury polynomial commitment schemes require a universal setup to generate the structured reference string (SRS). The setup is "universal" in the sense that a single setup can be reused across different circuits, and the same setup parameters can be shared with other KZG-based proof systems (such as Plonk and its variants).
L282: For production deployments, you should use parameters from a ceremony such as the 【95†Ethereum Perpetual Powers of Tau】, which has 80+ participants providing strong security guarantees (only one honest participant needed for security).
